screens.title: Transactions, Concurrency Control, and Locking
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why transactions are the unit of correctness in a database and how concurrency control preserves integrity when many clients operate at once. We'll ground the ideas in the ACID properties — atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability — and then show the S Q L commands you use to begin, commit, and rollback work. You will see common concurrency anomalies like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads, and understand how isolation levels change visibility and performance. We'll also look at locking behavior, lock granularity, and deadlocks, and end with a practical inventory-order transaction you can test. These skills matter because modern applications often run many simultaneous operations. Without transactions and proper locking, data can become inconsistent or lost. For a concrete example, imagine a bank transfer: if only one of two updates runs, money disappears or appears out of nowhere. As you go through the screens, notice the trade-offs between strong guarantees and concurrency, and prepare to apply the patterns that keep systems both correct and performant.

screens.title: What is a Transaction? ACID Overview
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction is a single logical unit of work that may read and write multiple rows and tables. The key claim is that a transaction behaves as if it is atomic: it either fully succeeds or leaves no effect. Atomicity protects you from partial updates. Consistency means every committed transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, obeying constraints such as foreign keys or check rules. Isolation is about concurrent visibility: other transactions should not see intermediate, uncommitted changes. Durability ensures that once a transaction commits, its changes survive process or power failures because they are written to persistent storage. An everyday example is a bank transfer that debits one account and credits another. If the second update fails, the system must roll back the entire transfer. A common misconception is to think durability guarantees an immediate physical disk write at commit; many systems use a durable log that guarantees recovery even if the in-memory state is not flushed instantly. To test understanding, ask: which ACID property matters most if a transfer partially applies? That property is atomicity. In practice you combine all four: atomic execution, validated consistency, isolation from other work, and durable commit.

keyIdea.title: ACID summary
keyIdea.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability together ensure correct, reliable transactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Transactions & ACID
Definition

Transaction

A transaction groups database operations into a single unit that must succeed or fail together.

Atomicity
All-or-nothing execution of a unit of work.
Consistency
Constraints and validation preserve valid states.
Isolation
Concurrent transactions behave as if run sequentially.
Durability
Committed changes survive failures.
Concrete Example
Bank transfer (concept)
Debit sender account and credit receiver account in one transaction so money is never lost or duplicated.
Common misconception
Durability does not mean the in-memory cache was flushed to disk before commit; it means the system can recover the committed state after a failure, typically via a write-ahead log.
Key Takeaway

Treat multi-step updates as a single unit so partial application cannot corrupt data.

screens.title: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK
screens.narratorSegment: You manage transaction boundaries with a few standard commands. BEGIN or START TRANSACTION marks the start. COMMIT makes all changes permanent. ROLLBACK undoes changes back to the start of the transaction. The important rule is to ensure every begin has a corresponding commit or rollback. A frequent mistake is to open a transaction and never close it; this can leave locks in place and block other clients. Consider the bank-transfer example: if an update to debit the sender succeeds but an update to credit the receiver fails, you must rollback to avoid inconsistent balances. The visual code panel shows a clear sequence: start the transaction, perform updates, check conditions, and then commit or rollback. In most application code, checks happen in the client or a stored procedure, and the result determines whether to commit. When you test, simulate both success and failure paths so locks and rollbacks behave as expected. Which step protects you from partial application? The combined use of BEGIN and ROLLBACK ensures atomicity. BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK means always pair begin with commit or rollback and test both success and failure paths to avoid lingering locks.. In practical terms, write transactions that commit or undo changes safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Transaction Commands
Code Example
<!-- Simple bank transfer (SQL-style) -->
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE Accounts
SET balance = balance - 100.00
WHERE account_id = 101;

-- check balance and other business rules here

UPDATE Accounts
SET balance = balance + 100.00
WHERE account_id = 102;

COMMIT;

-- If a check fails or an error occurs:
-- ROLLBACK;
Use explicit checks or application logic to decide whether to commit or rollback. Testing both paths is essential.
Explanation
  • BEGIN defines the boundary for atomic work.
  • COMMIT makes changes durable and visible to others.
  • ROLLBACK restores the state to before BEGIN if something fails.
Common mistake

Forgetting to commit or rollback leaves locks and can block other transactions.

Key Takeaway

Always ensure your application reaches a commit or rollback path for every transaction.

screens.title: Concurrency Anomalies
screens.narratorSegment: Concurrent transactions can observe each other's operations in different ways, leading to anomalies. A dirty read happens when Transaction A reads changes made by Transaction B before B commits. If B rolls back later, A has based work on data that never truly existed. A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction reads the same row twice and sees different values because another transaction committed a change in between those reads. A phantom read is similar but applies to sets of rows: a repeated query returns a different set because new rows were inserted or deleted by another committed transaction. These differences are important when you design application logic. For example, if you re-check a user's balance later in the same operation but a concurrent update changed it, you may make an incorrect decision. A common misconception is to assume that using a SELECT alone is always safe; without appropriate isolation, a plain SELECT can still return unstable values. To prevent specific anomalies you choose an isolation level that blocks the problematic visibility. Which anomaly matters for repeated row reads? Non-repeatable reads are the one you target with repeatable-read semantics.

keyIdea.text: Dirty reads show uncommitted changes; non-repeatable reads change single-row values; phantom reads change result sets.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Concurrency Anomalies
Dirty Read
Transaction reads uncommitted changes from another transaction.
Non-Repeatable Read
Same row read twice returns different values due to an intervening commit.
Phantom Read
A repeated query returns a different set because rows were inserted or deleted by another commit.
Concrete Scenarios
Dirty Read Example
T1 updates row but hasn't committed. T2 reads the updated value and acts on it. If T1 later rolls back, T2 used invalid input.
Non-Repeatable Read Example
T1 reads price, T2 updates price and commits, T1 reads price again and sees a different amount.
Phantom Read Example
T1 queries orders in a date range, T2 inserts a new order and commits. T1's repeated query now returns the new row.
Key Takeaway

Match your isolation level to the anomalies you must prevent. Lower isolation increases concurrency but allows more anomalies.

screens.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
screens.narratorSegment: Isolation levels control what a transaction can see of other transactions' work and thus which anomalies can occur. READ UNCOMMITTED is the weakest level: it allows dirty reads and offers maximum concurrency. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads; a transaction sees only committed changes, but non-repeatable and phantom reads remain possible. REPEATABLE READ prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads by presenting a consistent view of rows read, but phantom reads can still happen because sets can change. Finally, SERIALIZABLE is the strongest: it makes concurrent execution equivalent to some serial order, preventing dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads. The practical trade-off is performance: higher isolation typically reduces concurrency because the database must hold locks or use stricter snapshot semantics. Different systems implement these levels differently; for example, REPEATABLE READ is the default in some engines and has specific snapshot behavior. When choosing an isolation level, consider the application's tolerance for anomalies and its throughput needs. A common mistake is to assume the default isolation is always appropriate; evaluate the anomalies you must avoid and pick accordingly. Transaction Isolation Levels means higher isolation prevents more anomalies but reduces concurrency; choose based on correctness requirements and workload.. In practical terms, from read uncommitted to serializable and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Isolation Levels
READ UNCOMMITTED
Allows dirty reads. Highest concurrency, weakest guarantees.
READ COMMITTED
Prevents dirty reads. Default in many systems.
REPEATABLE READ
Prevents non-repeatable reads; phantom reads possible.
SERIALIZABLE
Prevents all read anomalies; strongest consistency, lowest concurrency.
Choosing an isolation level
  • Identify which anomalies would cause incorrect results for your application.
  • If phantom reads break your logic, prefer SERIALIZABLE or application-level compensation.
  • Balance throughput needs against data integrity requirements.

screens.title: Locking Basics: Shared and Exclusive Locks
screens.narratorSegment: Locks are the primary mechanism databases use to enforce isolation. A shared lock, sometimes called a read lock, allows multiple transactions to read the same resource concurrently but prevents writes. An exclusive lock, or write lock, prevents other transactions from reading or writing the locked resource. Lock granularity is the level at which locks are applied: row-level locks maximize concurrency because different transactions can modify different rows of the same table. Table-level locks are coarse and block many operations, which is appropriate for maintenance or bulk changes. Page-level locks sit between row and table in granularity. When designing transactions, prefer the smallest lock granularity that still protects correctness. A misconception is to think finer granularity always improves performance; in very high-throughput systems the overhead of many row locks can also cost C P U and coordination. The real design trade-off is concurrency versus lock management overhead. Also remember that some isolation implementations use multi-version concurrency control instead of locks for reads; the goal is the same: define what concurrent transactions can see. Locking Basics: Shared and Exclusive Locks means shared locks allow reads, exclusive locks block others; row-level locks increase concurrency but add management overhead.. In practical terms, how locks enforce isolation and why granularity matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Locking Basics
Shared (Read) Lock
Multiple readers allowed; writers blocked until shared locks release.
Exclusive (Write) Lock
Only one holder allowed; blocks both readers and writers.
Granularity
  • Row-level: highest concurrency.
  • Page-level: medium granularity.
  • Table-level: lowest concurrency, simplest coordination.
Concrete Consideration
Prefer row-level locks for OLTP workloads. Use table locks for maintenance or bulk DDL where simplicity matters more than concurrency.
Misconception
Finer-grained locks always improve throughput. In reality, lock overhead can grow with thousands of locked rows and hurt performance.
Key Takeaway

Select lock granularity to balance concurrency and coordination cost for your workload.

screens.title: Deadlocks and Avoidance
screens.narratorSegment: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait indefinitely for each other to release locks. A classic scenario involves Transaction A holding a lock on resource 1 and waiting for resource 2, while Transaction B holds resource 2 and waits for resource 1. Neither can proceed. Databases typically detect deadlocks and choose a victim to roll back, but prevention is better. A reliable strategy is to always access resources in a consistent order across transactions. If every transaction locks rows in primary key order, cyclic waits become unlikely. Keep transactions short to reduce the window where locks are held. Another tactic is to avoid user interaction inside a transaction; asking a user for input while locks are held can create long-duration locks. A common misconception is that deadlocks indicate a bug in the database; they are a normal consequence of concurrent locking. Designing transactions with consistent ordering and small scope reduces both the frequency and severity of deadlocks. When a deadlock victim occurs, ensure your application retries the operation safely. Deadlocks and Avoidance means access resources in a consistent order and keep transactions short to minimize deadlocks.. In practical terms, why deadlocks happen and how to minimize them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Deadlocks
Deadlock scenario
Transaction A locks Row 1 then requests Row 2. Transaction B locks Row 2 then requests Row 1. Both wait forever unless a system intervenes.
Prevention Strategies
  • Consistent locking order across transactions.
  • Keep transactions short and avoid long user interactions inside them.
  • Retry transactions when chosen as a deadlock victim.
Detection & Handling
Databases detect cycles and abort one transaction. Applications should be prepared to retry safely.
Key Takeaway

Plan resource ordering and short transactions; handle deadlock victims by retrying idempotently.

screens.title: Lock Granularity and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Lock granularity is a performance lever. Row-level locks maximize concurrency because different transactions can update different rows in the same table without interference. Page-level locks trade off by locking a block of rows together, reducing lock metadata but increasing contention for nearby rows. Table-level locks are simplest but the most restrictive: a single transaction can block many others. The practical choice depends on workload. High-concurrency OLTP systems benefit from row-level locks despite the overhead. Bulk operations, schema changes, or short maintenance windows often use table-level locks to simplify coordination. Also remember some engines use multi-version concurrency control for reads, avoiding read locks at the cost of keeping historical data versions. A misconception is to default to the finest granularity; measure lock contention and lock-management C P U to decide. Profiling your workload will reveal whether lock overhead or contention is the dominant cost. The design principle is to choose the smallest lock that meets correctness while keeping monitoring in place to detect hotspots. In practical terms, how row, page, and table locks affect throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Practical Transaction Management Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, reliable transactions follow a few steady patterns. Keep transactions short: lock time equals blocking time, so minimizing the code inside a transaction reduces contention. Do validations early: check funds or stock before performing updates so you can rollback quickly if a condition fails. Avoid interactive steps inside transactions such as waiting for user input. Use explicit error handling so any unexpected condition triggers a rollback. If your application retries a failed transaction, design the operation to be idempotent or tolerant of repeated execution to avoid double effects. When choosing an isolation level, pick the weakest level that prevents the anomalies you cannot tolerate. A common surprising issue is leaving an open transaction by failing to reach commit or rollback on every code path. To prevent this, ensure your frameworks or database drivers always close transactions in finally/finalize blocks. These patterns reduce contention, avoid deadlocks, and make your application robust in the face of concurrency. screens.title: Inventory Order Transaction (Starter SQL)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario simulates placing an order and demonstrates transaction control in practice. The operation must check a product's stock_quantity and, if enough, reduce the stock and insert an order record. If not enough stock exists, the transaction must rollback and leave the database unchanged. The starter S Q L creates Products and OrderLog tables and inserts sample data. In a client or stored procedure you would BEGIN a transaction, SELECT the current stock, evaluate the condition, and then UPDATE the Products table and INSERT into OrderLog before COMMIT. If any check fails or an exception occurs, you should ROLLBACK. When testing, run the scenario with sufficient stock then with insufficient stock and confirm that the rollback leaves the product quantity unchanged. A common misconception is to perform the SELECT and UPDATE in separate transactions; that allows races. Keep the check and update in the same transaction to prevent lost updates or overselling. Starter SQL
<!-- Create tables and sample data -->
CREATE TABLE Products (
  product_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_name VARCHAR(100),
  stock_quantity INT
);

CREATE TABLE OrderLog (
  log_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id INT,
  quantity_ordered INT,
  order_date TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  status VARCHAR(50)
);

INSERT INTO Products (product_id, product_name, stock_quantity) VALUES
(101, 'Laptop', 5),
(102, 'Mouse', 20);
Transaction Pattern (concept)
<!-- Pseudocode for the transactional order -->
BEGIN;
SELECT stock_quantity INTO current_stock FROM Products WHERE product_id = 101;
IF current_stock >= order_quantity THEN
  UPDATE Products SET stock_quantity = stock_quantity - order_quantity WHERE product_id = 101;
  INSERT INTO OrderLog (product_id, quantity_ordered, status) VALUES (101, order_quantity, 'Completed');
  COMMIT;
ELSE
  ROLLBACK;
END IF;
Try this

Test the transaction with order quantities that both succeed and fail. Confirm committed cases update stock and insert a log; rollbacks must leave stock unchanged.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring pitfalls can undermine transaction correctness. First, forgetting to COMMIT or ROLLBACK leaves open transactions and holds locks that block others. Always ensure your code path reaches a closing statement, typically in a finally block. Second, splitting a logical check and update across separate transactions invites races: a SELECT in one transaction followed by an UPDATE in another allows intervening commits. Keep checks and updates inside the same transaction. Third, assuming default isolation is sufficient can be hazardous; defaults vary and may allow anomalies you cannot tolerate. Fourth, assuming finer-grained locks always help is wrong; lock overhead can harm throughput for very busy systems. Finally, mishandling retries can double-apply updates; design idempotent operations or use unique tokens to detect duplicates. To avoid these problems, adopt simple rules: short transactions, validate early, always close transactions, choose appropriate isolation, and design retries carefully. As a reflective question, which of these pitfalls could silently break your application's invariants without throwing an error? That is the one you must prioritize in tests. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why transactions are the unit of correctness in a database and how concurrency control preserves integrity when many clients operate at once. We'll ground the ideas in the ACID properties — atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability — and then show the S Q L commands you use to begin, commit, and rollback work. You will see common concurrency anomalies like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads, and understand how isolation levels change visibility and performance. We'll also look at locking behavior, lock granularity, and deadlocks, and end with a practical inventory-order transaction you can test. These skills matter because modern applications often run many simultaneous operations. Without transactions and proper locking, data can become inconsistent or lost. For a concrete example, imagine a bank transfer: if only one of two updates runs, money disappears or appears out of nowhere. As you go through the screens, notice the trade-offs between strong guarantees and concurrency, and prepare to apply the patterns that keep systems both correct and performant.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you'll be able to explain and apply the ACID properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. That means you can reason about why a series of updates must commit together and what guarantees each property provides. Second, you'll implement transactions with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK, writing S Q L that ensures either full completion or safe rollback when checks fail. You'll practice a bank-transfer and an inventory order so the commands feel familiar. Third, you'll identify common concurrency problems — dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads — and map them to specific isolation levels that prevent them. Knowing the difference helps you choose the right trade-off for your application. Fourth, you'll understand locking strategies, lock granularity, and deadlock avoidance patterns so you can design transactions that minimize contention. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone to check that you can apply these ideas in a real scenario.

We will approach these objectives across four skill levels. First you will learn core definitions so you can name and explain ACID and basic locking. Next you will understand relationships: how isolation levels influence concurrency anomalies and how locks implement isolation. Then you will apply the ideas by writing transactions and choosing isolation levels in concrete scenarios such as an inventory update or a bank transfer. Finally, to master the topic you will reason about trade-offs: when SERIALIZABLE is necessary and when READ COMMITTED is more practical. Each milestone includes an example or small task so you can check the outcome yourself. For example, after implementing a transaction that updates stock and writes an order log, test both success and failure paths so you confirm rollback behavior. That concrete application step shifts the knowledge from description to working skill.

A transaction is a single logical unit of work that may read and write multiple rows and tables. The key claim is that a transaction behaves as if it is atomic: it either fully succeeds or leaves no effect. Atomicity protects you from partial updates. Consistency means every committed transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, obeying constraints such as foreign keys or check rules. Isolation is about concurrent visibility: other transactions should not see intermediate, uncommitted changes. Durability ensures that once a transaction commits, its changes survive process or power failures because they are written to persistent storage. An everyday example is a bank transfer that debits one account and credits another. If the second update fails, the system must roll back the entire transfer. A common misconception is to think durability guarantees an immediate physical disk write at commit; many systems use a durable log that guarantees recovery even if the in-memory state is not flushed instantly. To test understanding, ask: which ACID property matters most if a transfer partially applies? That property is atomicity. In practice you combine all four: atomic execution, validated consistency, isolation from other work, and durable commit.

You manage transaction boundaries with a few standard commands. BEGIN or START TRANSACTION marks the start. COMMIT makes all changes permanent. ROLLBACK undoes changes back to the start of the transaction. The important rule is to ensure every begin has a corresponding commit or rollback. A frequent mistake is to open a transaction and never close it; this can leave locks in place and block other clients. Consider the bank-transfer example: if an update to debit the sender succeeds but an update to credit the receiver fails, you must rollback to avoid inconsistent balances. The visual code panel shows a clear sequence: start the transaction, perform updates, check conditions, and then commit or rollback. In most application code, checks happen in the client or a stored procedure, and the result determines whether to commit. When you test, simulate both success and failure paths so locks and rollbacks behave as expected. Which step protects you from partial application? The combined use of BEGIN and ROLLBACK ensures atomicity. BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK means always pair begin with commit or rollback and test both success and failure paths to avoid lingering locks.. In practical terms, write transactions that commit or undo changes safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concurrent transactions can observe each other's operations in different ways, leading to anomalies. A dirty read happens when Transaction A reads changes made by Transaction B before B commits. If B rolls back later, A has based work on data that never truly existed. A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction reads the same row twice and sees different values because another transaction committed a change in between those reads. A phantom read is similar but applies to sets of rows: a repeated query returns a different set because new rows were inserted or deleted by another committed transaction. These differences are important when you design application logic. For example, if you re-check a user's balance later in the same operation but a concurrent update changed it, you may make an incorrect decision. A common misconception is to assume that using a SELECT alone is always safe; without appropriate isolation, a plain SELECT can still return unstable values. To prevent specific anomalies you choose an isolation level that blocks the problematic visibility. Which anomaly matters for repeated row reads? Non-repeatable reads are the one you target with repeatable-read semantics.

Isolation levels control what a transaction can see of other transactions' work and thus which anomalies can occur. READ UNCOMMITTED is the weakest level: it allows dirty reads and offers maximum concurrency. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads; a transaction sees only committed changes, but non-repeatable and phantom reads remain possible. REPEATABLE READ prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads by presenting a consistent view of rows read, but phantom reads can still happen because sets can change. Finally, SERIALIZABLE is the strongest: it makes concurrent execution equivalent to some serial order, preventing dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads. The practical trade-off is performance: higher isolation typically reduces concurrency because the database must hold locks or use stricter snapshot semantics. Different systems implement these levels differently; for example, REPEATABLE READ is the default in some engines and has specific snapshot behavior. When choosing an isolation level, consider the application's tolerance for anomalies and its throughput needs. A common mistake is to assume the default isolation is always appropriate; evaluate the anomalies you must avoid and pick accordingly. Transaction Isolation Levels means higher isolation prevents more anomalies but reduces concurrency; choose based on correctness requirements and workload.. In practical terms, from read uncommitted to serializable and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Locks are the primary mechanism databases use to enforce isolation. A shared lock, sometimes called a read lock, allows multiple transactions to read the same resource concurrently but prevents writes. An exclusive lock, or write lock, prevents other transactions from reading or writing the locked resource. Lock granularity is the level at which locks are applied: row-level locks maximize concurrency because different transactions can modify different rows of the same table. Table-level locks are coarse and block many operations, which is appropriate for maintenance or bulk changes. Page-level locks sit between row and table in granularity. When designing transactions, prefer the smallest lock granularity that still protects correctness. A misconception is to think finer granularity always improves performance; in very high-throughput systems the overhead of many row locks can also cost C P U and coordination. The real design trade-off is concurrency versus lock management overhead. Also remember that some isolation implementations use multi-version concurrency control instead of locks for reads; the goal is the same: define what concurrent transactions can see. Locking Basics: Shared and Exclusive Locks means shared locks allow reads, exclusive locks block others; row-level locks increase concurrency but add management overhead.. In practical terms, how locks enforce isolation and why granularity matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A deadlock occurs when transactions wait indefinitely for each other to release locks. A classic scenario involves Transaction A holding a lock on resource 1 and waiting for resource 2, while Transaction B holds resource 2 and waits for resource 1. Neither can proceed. Databases typically detect deadlocks and choose a victim to roll back, but prevention is better. A reliable strategy is to always access resources in a consistent order across transactions. If every transaction locks rows in primary key order, cyclic waits become unlikely. Keep transactions short to reduce the window where locks are held. Another tactic is to avoid user interaction inside a transaction; asking a user for input while locks are held can create long-duration locks. A common misconception is that deadlocks indicate a bug in the database; they are a normal consequence of concurrent locking. Designing transactions with consistent ordering and small scope reduces both the frequency and severity of deadlocks. When a deadlock victim occurs, ensure your application retries the operation safely. Deadlocks and Avoidance means access resources in a consistent order and keep transactions short to minimize deadlocks.. In practical terms, why deadlocks happen and how to minimize them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lock granularity is a performance lever. Row-level locks maximize concurrency because different transactions can update different rows in the same table without interference. Page-level locks trade off by locking a block of rows together, reducing lock metadata but increasing contention for nearby rows. Table-level locks are simplest but the most restrictive: a single transaction can block many others. The practical choice depends on workload. High-concurrency OLTP systems benefit from row-level locks despite the overhead. Bulk operations, schema changes, or short maintenance windows often use table-level locks to simplify coordination. Also remember some engines use multi-version concurrency control for reads, avoiding read locks at the cost of keeping historical data versions. A misconception is to default to the finest granularity; measure lock contention and lock-management C P U to decide. Profiling your workload will reveal whether lock overhead or contention is the dominant cost. In practice, reliable transactions follow a few steady patterns. Keep transactions short: lock time equals blocking time, so minimizing the code inside a transaction reduces contention. Do validations early: check funds or stock before performing updates so you can rollback quickly if a condition fails. Avoid interactive steps inside transactions such as waiting for user input. Use explicit error handling so any unexpected condition triggers a rollback. If your application retries a failed transaction, design the operation to be idempotent or tolerant of repeated execution to avoid double effects. When choosing an isolation level, pick the weakest level that prevents the anomalies you cannot tolerate. A common surprising issue is leaving an open transaction by failing to reach commit or rollback on every code path. To prevent this, ensure your frameworks or database drivers always close transactions in finally/finalize blocks. These patterns reduce contention, avoid deadlocks, and make your application robust in the face of concurrency. Several recurring pitfalls can undermine transaction correctness. First, forgetting to COMMIT or ROLLBACK leaves open transactions and holds locks that block others. Always ensure your code path reaches a closing statement, typically in a finally block. Second, splitting a logical check and update across separate transactions invites races: a SELECT in one transaction followed by an UPDATE in another allows intervening commits. Keep checks and updates inside the same transaction. Third, assuming default isolation is sufficient can be hazardous; defaults vary and may allow anomalies you cannot tolerate. Fourth, assuming finer-grained locks always help is wrong; lock overhead can harm throughput for very busy systems. Finally, mishandling retries can double-apply updates; design idempotent operations or use unique tokens to detect duplicates. To avoid these problems, adopt simple rules: short transactions, validate early, always close transactions, choose appropriate isolation, and design retries carefully. These three cards summarize the essential ideas. First, a transaction is a single logical unit that must meet ACID properties so multi-step updates are correct and durable. Second, isolation levels control what concurrent transactions see; higher levels prevent more anomalies but reduce concurrency. Third, locking and lock granularity are the mechanisms that enforce isolation; consistent resource ordering and short transactions reduce deadlocks. Keep these ideas in mind as a checklist when you design transactional code: bundle related operations in a transaction, choose the isolation level based on the anomalies you must avoid, and pick lock granularity that balances concurrency and overhead. Finally, always test both successful and failing transaction paths so commit and rollback behave as expected.
